name: The contemplative ideal and the origin of 'theory'
plain_explanation: Pythagoras taught that the best kind of life is neither buying and selling nor competing, but simply looking on -- disinterested contemplation, especially of mathematical truths -- which he considered the highest form of purification of the soul.
precise_definition: An ethical and metaphysical doctrine, summarized by Russell via Burnet's account of the 'three kinds of men' at the Olympic Games, holding that disinterested intellectual contemplation ('theoria') is the greatest purification and the truest philosophy, releasing the soul from the 'wheel of birth'.
why_it_mattered: This ideal gave the pursuit of pure (non-applied) mathematics unprecedented prestige, and, in Russell's view, is the historical source of the enduring Western association between disinterested truth, the contemplative life, and philosophical/theological dignity.
historical_origin: A specifically Pythagorean transformation of the originally Orphic, ecstatic sense of 'theoria' into an intellectual, mathematical sense.
examples: Burnet's analogy of three types of visitors to the Olympic Games: those who buy and sell, those who compete, and those who simply look on (the highest)
competing_positions: Modern, industrial/pragmatist values that esteem the active competitor (the 'player') over the contemplative spectator
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell connects this directly to the long philosophical prestige of the 'gentleman'/contemplative ideal, which depended historically on a society resting on slave labor.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious: contemplation is presented as a path to salvation from the cycle of rebirth.
